Read the following notes from our operations handbook carefully.

A load balancer sits in front of several copies of the same service and spreads incoming requests between them. If one copy stops answering its health check, the balancer stops sending it traffic until it recovers. This keeps the service available while individual servers are restarted or replaced, but it also hides problems: users may see nothing wrong while one server has been failing for hours, so the health checks themselves need to be watched and tested regularly.

Time synchronisation is easy to forget until something goes wrong. When the clocks on two servers differ by more than a few seconds, log lines no longer line up, tokens that carry an expiry time are rejected as not yet valid or already expired, and graphs from different machines show events in the wrong order. Running a time service on every node and checking its offset regularly is a small cost that removes a whole class of confusing faults.

Persistent storage in a cluster is provided by volumes that outlive the pods that use them. A database pod that is deleted and recreated should find its data exactly as it left it, which is why the volume is claimed separately and the claim is retained when the pod goes away. Deleting the claim by mistake destroys the data, so operations that touch storage deserve a second pair of eyes and a recent backup that has actually been restored at least once.

Network policies decide which pods may talk to which other pods. A sensible starting point is to deny everything and then allow only the specific paths that are needed, such as the website reaching the API, or the worker reaching the database and the model server. The benefit is that a compromised or misconfigured pod cannot wander across the cluster. The cost is that a missing rule shows up as a silent timeout, which can be hard to tell from a slow server.

Sealed secrets let a team keep encrypted credentials in the same repository as the rest of the configuration. Only the cluster holds the key that can decrypt them, and each secret is locked to a particular name and namespace, so copying one to another place does not work. This keeps passwords out of plain text and out of chat messages, but it means that a new namespace needs its own freshly sealed copy of every secret it uses.

Resource requests and limits tell the scheduler how much processor time and memory a container needs and how much it may use. When the request equals the limit the container is guaranteed that share and cannot borrow from its neighbours, which makes measurements repeatable. When limits are missing, one busy pod can slow down everything else on the node, and a pod that exceeds its memory limit is killed and restarted, which looks like a mysterious crash if nobody checks the reason.

Continuous integration builds the software automatically whenever the code changes, runs a quick set of checks, and publishes the result as a container image with a tag that names the exact commit. Deployments then refer to that tag or to its digest, so everyone can say precisely which version ran. A merge that does not update the tag in the deployment file changes nothing in the cluster, which surprises people the first time it happens.

Monitoring works best when it records raw numbers with their timestamps and leaves the interpretation to people. A graph of memory use that climbs steadily for a day before a restart points to a leak, while a sudden step usually points to a deployment or a change in load. Alerts should be few and meaningful: a flood of warnings teaches people to ignore them, and the one that matters is lost among the rest.
